incident.originalFailure: The provider catalog test expected exactly one system/models/refresh request. The filtered request list was empty. The refreshed default was b, the editor remained on a, the edited model remained selected, and Apply was disabled.
incident.limits: The hosted snapshot shows the final UI after a timeout. It cannot identify which commit-phase interleaving occurred in that individual run.

catalogEvidence.scenario: React Profiler invokes a fresh confirmation on the first interactive commit after a different default provider and registry revision arrive. Verify the old consent does not authorize writes and the fresh consent survives passive effects to permit exactly one write for the original provider a at r2.

baseline.reason: The Apply button was still disabled after the new consent.

catalogEvidence.scope: Deterministic component-level React commit ordering; distinct from a physical-user latency measurement.

profileEvidence.scenario: The user sees no connections scheduled for removal at r1. The registry response is held. A cached profile remains visible. The test attempts to check confirmation, then releases r2 where the restoration preview lists new-connection for removal. It observes whether either restore or delete can be submitted before fresh consent.
profileEvidence.browserEnvironment: Desktop Microsoft Edge, actual DOM and real ProviderSettings/ProviderProfiles. Local controlled API only. Synthetic provider identifiers, no real account or provider service.

newRegressionCases: restore consent during delayed registry refresh
delete consent during delayed registry refresh
same visible profile on a different registry revision without a loading transition

profileEvidence.impact: The restore target profile ID is unchanged, but the set of current connections that would be removed can change between previews. The delete scenario uses the same stale approval and still targets its selected immutable profile ID.

distinction: The catalog defect can erase a valid new approval and suppress the intended write. The profile defect can retain an old approval and allow a later revision to be written without checking its new preview. The catalog assertion was the sole reported Linux Vitest failure; the separate profile defect was discovered during adjacent-code review.
